reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A form of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia mediated by IgM autoantibodies that bind red cells optimally at cold temperatures
Symptoms worsen on cold exposure and include acrocyanosis and mottling of the extremities, ears and nose, with haemolytic anaemia
The direct antiglobulin test is positive for complement (C3d) and negative or weak for IgG, reflecting complement-mediated haemolysis
Cold agglutinins cause red cell clumping that can spuriously raise the mean cell volume and confound automated counts unless the sample is warmed
Primary cold agglutinin disease is associated with a clonal low-grade B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder of the bone marrow
Secondary cold agglutinin syndrome may follow infections such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Epstein-Barr virus, or accompany lymphoma
Cornerstones of management are cold avoidance and keeping the patient warm, with rituximab-based therapy for significant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Cold agglutinin disease is caused by monoclonal (in primary disease) or polyclonal (in secondary disease) IgM autoantibodies, usually directed against the I antigen on red cells, that bind most avidly in the cooler peripheral circulation. Antibody binding fixes complement on the red cell surface; as cells return to the warmer core the IgM detaches but deposited complement drives predominantly extravascular clearance by the liver, with some intravascular haemolysis. Agglutination of red cells in cold peripheral vessels also produces the circulatory symptoms. In primary disease a clonal marrow B-cell lymphoproliferative process produces the pathogenic monoclonal IgM.
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test with monospecific reagents (C3d and IgG)
Cold agglutinin titre and thermal amplitude
Blood film and warmed sample to correct agglutination artefact
Haemolysis markers (reticulocytes, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin)
Serum protein electrophoresis and marrow assessment for a clonal B-cell disorder
Screening for underlying infection or lymphoma in secondary disease
redFlags: Severe or rapidly falling haemoglobin requiring transfusion
Acute exacerbation on cold exposure with cardiovascular compromise
Features suggesting underlying lymphoma requiring investigation
reference.prognosis: Primary cold agglutinin disease is usually chronic; many patients have mild, manageable haemolysis while others need directed therapy, and prognosis is also shaped by any underlying lymphoproliferative disorder. Secondary post-infectious cases are often self-limiting.
pitfalls: Being misled by spurious red cell indices from cold-induced agglutination in unwarmed samples
Using warm-antibody treatments such as corticosteroids and splenectomy, which are relatively ineffective here
Transfusing without warming blood and the patient, worsening haemolysis
Failing to investigate for an underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder
